title: Koko has piles of bananas and h hours before the guards return. Each hour she eats up to a chosen speed k bananas from one pile. Find the minimum integer speed k such that she can finish all piles within h hours. Run in logarithmic time over the speed.
shortTitle: Koko Eating Bananas: Binary Search on the Answer With a Feasibility Check
keyPoints: Binary-search the answer (the speed), not an array: the search space is 1 to max(piles)
Feasibility function computes hours needed at a given speed; feasibility is monotonic
Ceiling division without floating point: (pile + speed - 1) / speed
Lower-bound search pattern: on feasible, try smaller (high = mid); on infeasible, go faster (low = mid + 1)
Time is O(n * log(max pile)) where n is the number of piles
The pattern generalizes to any optimization problem with a monotonic feasibility condition

s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search the answer itself, using a yes-or-no feasibility check that is monotonic.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Binary search on the answer** – instead of searching an array, search the space of possible answers (eating speeds) for the minimum that satisfies a condition.
- **Feasibility function** – computes hours needed at a given speed; the condition is that the hours do not exceed the deadline.
- **Monotonicity** – if speed K finishes in time, every speed greater than K also finishes; if K is too slow, every slower speed is also too slow.
- **Ceiling division** – (pile + speed - 1) / speed avoids floating-point error and stays exact.
- **Complexity** – O(n * log(max pile)) where n is the number of piles.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must clear a backlog of transaction batches before a regulatory cutoff. It can set a processing rate: how many items per hour each worker handles. A higher rate clears the backlog faster but costs more compute. The manager binary-searches the rate: pick a middle rate, compute whether the backlog clears in time, and if it does, try lower to save resources; if not, raise the rate.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Koko Eating Bananas is the textbook example of binary search on the answer, a technique where you search the space of possible answers rather than an array. The feasibility function computes how many hours Koko needs at a given speed by summing ceiling divisions. Feasibility is monotonic: faster speeds never need more hours, so a clean yes-or-no boundary exists for binary search to find.

The lower-bound search pattern converges on the minimum feasible speed: when feasible, try slower (high = mid); when infeasible, go faster (low = mid + 1). Ceiling division with integers, (pile + speed - 1) / speed, avoids floating-point rounding errors that could miscount hours before a compliance deadline.

The real value of mastering this problem is the template. Any optimization problem where a monotonic yes-or-no condition partitions the search space can be solved with binary search on the answer: ship packages within D days (search capacity), split array minimizing the largest sum (search the threshold), or aggressive cows (search the minimum distance).

In the batch clearing system at the National Bank of India, the batches are the piles, the regulatory cutoff is the hour budget, and the processing rate is the eating speed. Finding the minimum feasible rate directly saves compute costs. The ceiling-division trick keeps the calculation exact, and the O(n * log(max_pile)) time handles large batch pools within the scheduling window.

Remember one sentence: binary-search the candidate speed, check feasibility with ceiling division, and the monotonic boundary gives the minimum rate that clears everything in time.
